newsitem.title: USA: Astra USA ex-CEO pleads not guilty.
newsitem.headline: Astra USA ex-CEO pleads not guilty.

text.p: Lars Bildman, the former chief executive of Astra Ab unit Astra USA, plead not guilty on Wednesday in a federal court to 35 charges including fraud and tax evasion.
Special assistant U.S. Attorney Stephen Huggard said that Bildman, 51, posed a serious risk of flight from the country.

Bildman's two homes in the United States are both up for sale, he has access to 10 or 11 foreign bank accounts and his native Sweden does not have an extradition treaty with the United States for his alleged crimes, Huggard said.
Furthermore, the evidence against Bildman is "quite strong" and he faces years in prison if convicted, he said.
Despite the risk of flight, U.S. prosecutors and the defense agreed to a deal to release Bildman on bail of $1.6 million and be confined to his "Viking's Retreat" vacation home in Killington, Vt.
But U.S. Magistrate Judge Charles Swartwood advised the defense to find a place in Massachusetts for Bildman and took the question of bail under advisement.
"There's some real problems of him going to Killington, Vt.," he said. "Killington is close to the Canadian border."
The 35 charges against Bildman include charges of conspiracy, mail fraud, wire fraud, filing false tax returns and violating interstate travel in the furtherance of prostitution.
He was fired from Astra last year after a Business Week article exposed allegations of widespread sexual harassment and other abuses at the company.
U.S. Attorney Donald Stern told reporters after the hearing that the investigation into Astra is continuing and may lead to additional charges against Bildman or others.

Huggard said the $1.6 million bail would be secured by a $300,000 mortgage on Bildman's home in the Boston suburb of Brookline, Mass. Bildman's wife is currently in the process of divorce proceedings and lives in the Brookline home, he said.
The remaining $1.3 million in bail would be secured by Bildman's share of his estimated $2.5 million retirement funds, Huggard said.

If found guilty, Bildman faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine for each count of conspiracy, mail fraud, wire fraud and interstate travel. He faces up to three years and a $250,000 fine for each count of the tax charges.
The case is scheduled to go to trial on June 23 in Worcester, Mass.
